text: I think we live in a throwaway culture. Products are cheap and often designed to break after a couple of years, so it seems easier to buy a new one than to repair the old one. On top of that, advertising constantly persuades us that we need the latest model. The result is mountains of waste, especially electronic waste, which is hard to recycle.

text: Yes, I believe regulation is the only realistic way. If it's left to the companies, many of them will keep using plastic because it's cheap. Of course, there would be a transition period, but customers would adapt quickly, as happened with plastic bags in supermarkets. Eventually, I think people might even prefer less packaging, because it looks more eco-friendly.

text: In theory, yes, but not any time soon. Solar and wind power depend on the weather, so we need better ways of storing energy, and that's still expensive. Besides, the infrastructure for oil and gas has been built over a century. I reckon we'll see a gradual shift, with renewables covering more and more of our needs year by year.

text: There are quite a few options. Planting more trees and creating parks would improve air quality and make cities more pleasant to live in. Another idea is encouraging cycling by building proper bike lanes. If I had to choose one, I'd pick public transport, because reducing the number of cars would have the biggest impact on both pollution and noise.
